**edulab** is a set of throwaway prototypes exploring how a user can *learn* from an agent that is doing their work for them, rather than passively watching it. See `notes/exploration.md` for the thinking and the prototype ladder, and `notes/studies.md` for the supporting literature.

Everything here is a demo, and the scaffolding constraints are deliberate. No database, no auth, no persistence, no configuration, no router. All state is client-side and in memory, discarded on refresh. The backend holds no conversation state: it is a pipe from the websocket to the Anthropic SDK, and inference is streamed rather than awaited so the demo reads as a real agent session instead of a latency pause. The agentic loop is a heavily simplified take on `~/src/magenta.nvim` (anthropic only, api key only, no MCP); the web setup is lifted from `~/src/gatherus/`.

# Layout

- **`packages/iso/protocol.ts`** — the websocket message union (`ClientMessage`, `ServerFrame`). Imported by both sides.
- **`packages/backend/`** — Fastify server, entry `app.ts` (reads `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` from the root `.env`, listens on 3000). `socket.ts` registers `GET /api/socket` and is a **pipe**: it forwards the client's `MessageCreateParamsStreaming` to the SDK unexamined and streams `RawMessageStreamEvent`s back. It holds no conversation state.
- **`packages/frontend/`** — entry `main.ts`, which mounts `prototypes/chat.ts` into the page. There is one prototype and no router; later ideas land as new actions inside it rather than as separate pages. The sample picker lives in the header bar next to the layer navigation, and switching sample is a full page load.
  - `prototypes/chat.ts` — owns the thread tree, the state, and the single dispatch loop.
  - `conversation.ts` — the `MessageParam[]` plus the stream accumulator. Model, max tokens, and the system prompt are module constants here. The system prompt is deliberately **task mode**, not tutoring: learning mode is what we layer on top of the transcript it produces.
  - `view.ts` — the transcript and composer. `vamp.ts` is copied verbatim from gatherus.
- **`packages/e2e/`** — Playwright specs (`.spec.ts`, so vitest's `packages/**/*.test.ts` glob ignores them).
- **`docs/transcripts/`** — synced magenta thread archives, raw material for the prototypes. Refresh with `npm run sync:transcripts`.
- **`notes/exploration.md`** — the framing. What the learning problem actually is, why the obvious moves (student modeling, agent-as-tutor) are traps, and what we are deliberately not building. **Read this before proposing a direction or adding a prototype.** The numbered prototype sketches at the end are the roadmap.
- **`plans/`** — implementation plans, annotated with what actually happened as each stage landed.

# Commands

- `npm run dev` — vite on **5173** plus the backend on **3000**. Open http://localhost:5173. `/api/` (including the websocket) is proxied.
- `npm test` — vitest, node environment. The only unit tests are over the stream accumulator.
- `npm run test:e2e` — Playwright on its own ports (5174/3100). UI specs stub the socket with `page.routeWebSocket`, so they need no API key; `smoke.spec.ts` hits the real API and is skipped without `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`.
- `npm run sync:transcripts` — re-run `scripts/sync-transcripts.sh` to pull magenta thread archives whose `cwd` is this repo into `docs/transcripts/`. Incremental: existing threads are updated in place, so it is safe to re-run any time.
- `npm run typecheck` — `tsc --noEmit` across every package. Always run this rather than a bare `tsc`.
- `npm run lint` / `npm run lint:fix` — biome.

# Conventions

**Use the type system.** Disjoint unions over optional fields, exhaustive switches, branded ids. Prefer nominal/branded types over bare strings wherever a string is really an identifier — including map and record *keys* (`Record<ToolName, Tool>`, not `Record<string, Tool>`).

**Simplicity over abstraction.** This is prototype code with a short life. Write the concrete thing; do not build a provider abstraction or a plugin system for a second case that may never arrive. `@anthropic-ai/sdk` types are used directly rather than wrapped.

**Explicit over silent.** `RawMessageStreamEvent` is an open union we forward verbatim, so unhandled variants `console.warn` rather than throwing — but "we chose to ignore this" and "we have never heard of this" must be different branches (see `conversation.ts`).

**Single dispatch per prototype.** Each `prototypes/*.ts` owns one `dispatch` loop that calls `update` then `view.sync`. Views never hold their own dispatch. See the **[vamp skill](.magenta/skills/vamp/skill.md)** before writing any view code.

**Tests sit beside the module they assert** (`conversation.test.ts` next to `conversation.ts`), not beside the transport that reaches it. Views are verified in a real browser via Playwright, not jsdom.

**`~/src/magenta.nvim`** is a reference implementation for the agentic loop (`node/core/src/providers/`) if this outgrows itself. Do not copy from it wholesale.

# Objective and Context

Verbatim request:

> I want to update the way we generate the knowledge graph from the session.
>
> - rather than pushing the entire thread tree in at once, I want to instead do a traversal of the threads one at a time. We will traverse each thread in the tree in a dfs order.

This replaces the one-shot extraction that landed in `plans/2026-09-05-domain-graph.md`. That pass rendered the whole tree into a single seed and asked one thread to map the session; it is a single enormous prompt whose output quality is unobservable, and it gives the model no reason to attend to any particular thing the user said. The unit of evidence about what a user understands is **one user turn**, so that becomes the unit of extraction.

## Entities

- `Interaction` — one user turn somewhere in the tree, together with the little context needed to read it: where it sits (the breadcrumb of origin passages down to it), what the agent had just said, and what the agent said back. New; lives in `interactions.ts`.
- `interactions(tree)` — pure `ThreadTree -> Interaction[]`, DFS, parents before children.
- `REFLECT_SYSTEM` / `reflectPrompt(interaction, graph)` — the per-interaction prompt, replacing `EXTRACT_SYSTEM` / `renderTree`.
- `runThread` (`thread.ts`) — the programmatic interface each reflection runs through; unattended, tools client side, settles on `yield`.
- `Build` (`graph-view.ts`) — gains progress, since the run is now N threads rather than one.

## Relevant files

- `packages/frontend/threads.ts` — `ThreadTree`, `TreeNode { origin, thread, children }`. The tree being walked; unchanged.
- `packages/frontend/thread.ts` — `runThread(socket, { prompt, system, tools, yieldSchema })`, `Message`, `Thread`. Unchanged.
- `packages/frontend/prompt.ts` — owns `EXTRACT_SYSTEM`, `renderTree`, `transcript`, `line`, `actionLabel`. `EXTRACT_SYSTEM`/`renderTree` are replaced here; `transcript`/`line` are reused by `interactions.ts` rendering.
- `packages/frontend/selection.ts` — `Anchor`, `anchorText(anchor, messages)`, `ThreadId`.
- `packages/frontend/graph.ts` / `graph-tools.ts` — `KnowledgeGraph.render()`, `writeTools(graph)`. Unchanged.
- `packages/frontend/prototypes/chat.ts` — `runBuild()`, the one wiring point. Becomes a sequential loop.
- `packages/frontend/graph-view.ts` — the toolbar, `Build`, the status line.
- `packages/e2e/tests/graph.spec.ts` — stubs the socket and asserts the tools -> graph -> canvas path.

# Design

**Slice the tree into interactions.** `interactions(tree)` walks depth-first from the root, parents before children, and emits one `Interaction` per user turn. Two kinds of user turn exist and both must be captured:

- A typed turn: a `{ type: "text", role: "user" }` entry in a thread's `messages`.
- The synthetic opening of a learning thread. `Thread.messages` deliberately excludes the seed, so a child thread's first interaction is reconstructed from its `origin`: the passage the user highlighted plus `actionLabel(origin.action)`. That highlight *is* the strongest single piece of evidence in the session — the user pointing at a line and saying they do not understand it — so losing it would gut the extraction.

**Context is bounded, not cumulative.** Sending the thread-so-far with every interaction is quadratic in tokens and drowns the turn we actually care about. Each `Interaction` instead carries:

- `breadcrumb` — the chain of `"<quote>" - <action label>` from the root down to this thread. Cheap, and it is what tells the model this exchange is a follow-up on a specific passage rather than free-floating.
- `before` — the assistant blocks between the previous user turn and this one, i.e. exactly the text the user was reacting to. Bounded, and it does not accumulate down the thread.
- `text` — the user's turn, the thing under the microscope.
- `after` — the assistant blocks that answered it. Needed because a quiz answer only means something next to the question, and because the agent's explanation is what the user's *next* turn will react to.

Root-thread turn 0 has an empty `breadcrumb` and empty `before`: the task request is the origin of everything and needs no framing.

**One thread per interaction, run sequentially.** `runBuild()` becomes a `for` loop over `interactions(tree)`, each iteration a `runThread(socket, { system: REFLECT_SYSTEM, prompt: reflectPrompt(interaction, graph.render()), tools: writeTools(graph), yieldSchema: "text" })`. Sequential, not `Promise.all`: the whole point is that each reflection sees the graph the previous ones built, so that the second mention of a concept updates a node instead of minting a rival for it. Concurrency here would produce a duplicate-ridden graph and there is no latency budget to defend — the user watches nodes appear, which is a better progress bar than a spinner.

`graph.render()` is re-read inside the loop, per iteration, so each prompt carries the current overview. The yielded text is discarded; the graph is the output, exactly as before. A failed reflection is recorded and the loop **continues** — one bad turn should not abandon the other thirty — and the count of failures surfaces in the status line.

**The prompt is a reflection, not an extraction.** `REFLECT_SYSTEM` reframes the job: you are looking at one exchange, in the context of a graph that already exists; ask what domain concepts this exchange touches, whether they are in the graph, what understanding the user demonstrated, and whether anything here reads as a gap or a misconception. Then the restraint clauses, which are the ones that actually control output size: touch only what this interaction is about; keep the graph small and coarse; split a concept only when the split expresses something real about this user's understanding; a concept the user merely brushed past does not need a node.

Alternatives rejected: a single thread walked through the interactions as a conversation (the context grows without bound and later turns get worse, which is the current problem in a new shape); parallel reflections with a merge pass (a merge pass is a second extraction problem, and duplicate concepts are exactly what the sequential graph-in-the-prompt already prevents).

## Interfaces

```ts
// interactions.ts
/** One user turn, with the bounded context needed to read it. The unit of
 * evidence about what this user understands. */
export type Interaction = {
  thread: ThreadId;
  /** Root first: the chain of highlighted passages and asks that led here.
   * Empty for the root task thread. */
  breadcrumb: ReadonlyArray<{ quote: string; ask: string }>;
  /** How this turn came about: the user typed it, or it is the synthetic
   * opening of a learning thread, reconstructed from the thread's origin. */
  kind: "typed" | "opening";
  /** The assistant blocks the user was reacting to; empty for the first turn
   * of any thread. */
  before: ReadonlyArray<Message>;
  /** For "opening", the action label; for "typed", the turn's text. */
  text: string;
  /** The assistant blocks that answered it; empty if nothing came back yet. */
  after: ReadonlyArray<Message>;
};

/** Depth-first over the tree, parents before children, in creation order. */
export function interactions(tree: ThreadTree): ReadonlyArray<Interaction>;
```

```ts
// prompt.ts (replacing EXTRACT_SYSTEM and renderTree)
export const REFLECT_SYSTEM: string;
/** The interaction, its context, and the current graph overview. */
export function reflectPrompt(interaction: Interaction, graph: string): string;
```

```ts
// graph-view.ts
export type Build =
  | { type: "idle" }
  | { type: "running"; done: number; total: number }
  | { type: "done"; failed: number }
  | { type: "error"; error: string };
```

## Invariants

- Every user turn in the tree produces exactly one `Interaction`, and every learning thread contributes its opening even though `Thread.messages` never shows it. Nothing is counted twice.
- Order is DFS, parents before children, children in creation order. A child's opening is reflected on after the parent turn that spawned it, so the graph is built in the order the user actually learned.
- Reflections run one at a time and each one's prompt carries the graph as left by the previous. Nothing overlaps.
- A failed reflection does not abort the run and does not corrupt the graph; the graph is only ever changed through the tools.
- `interactions` is pure and does not touch the graph, the socket, or any thread state.
- The extraction still writes only through `writeTools`; no new mutation path.
- Re-running the build extends the graph rather than duplicating it, exactly as the one-shot pass claimed to.

# Stages

## slicing the tree into interactions

- Goal: `interactions(tree)` exists and is exercised in isolation. Nothing consumes it yet.
- Tests (`interactions.test.ts`, building trees over the `FakeSocket` the way `threads.test.ts` does):
  - A root thread with two user turns yields two interactions, each carrying the assistant blocks that immediately preceded and followed it, and neither carrying the other's.
  - A child thread contributes an opening interaction whose `text` is the action label and whose `breadcrumb` ends with the highlighted passage — the case that would silently vanish if we only read `messages`.
  - A grandchild's breadcrumb has both ancestors' quotes, root first.
  - Order over a root with two children, one of which has a child, is DFS parents-first in creation order.
  - A turn that is still streaming (no assistant reply yet) yields an interaction with an empty `after` rather than being skipped.

## the reflection prompt

- Goal: `REFLECT_SYSTEM` and `reflectPrompt` replace `EXTRACT_SYSTEM` and `renderTree`, which are deleted along with their tests.
- Tests (`prompt.test.ts`):
  - `reflectPrompt` puts the user's turn, the surrounding assistant blocks and the rendered graph in the output, and an opening interaction renders its quote and its ask.
  - A root-thread interaction with no breadcrumb renders without an empty framing section.
  - `REFLECT_SYSTEM` states the scope restriction and the coarseness rule — these are the clauses the whole design rests on, so their absence should fail a test rather than quietly degrade every graph.

## sequential build

- Goal: the button runs one reflection per interaction, in order, and the canvas fills in as it goes.
- `runBuild()` loops over `interactions(tree)`, awaiting each `runThread`, re-reading `graph.render()` per iteration, syncing the view after each so nodes appear progressively. Failures increment a counter and the loop continues.
- The toolbar shows `reflecting on interaction 3 of 12`, and `done (1 failed)` when a reflection errored.
- Tests:
  - `packages/e2e/tests/graph.spec.ts`: a stubbed backend that answers each request with a `put_nodes` call plus a `yield`, over a session with a root thread and one learning thread. Assert the number of requests equals the number of interactions, that the requests arrive one at a time (the stub records overlap), and that the canvas ends with the nodes from all of them. This is the stage's real risk — a loop that fires everything at once, or that stops at the first error, both still "work" in a unit test.
  - `packages/e2e/tests/graph.spec.ts`: a backend that errors on the second reflection still finishes the rest and reports `1 failed`.

To actually get the cache hit, `reflectPrompt` returns content blocks rather than one string: base prompt, seed and prefix as one text block carrying `cache_control: { type: "ephemeral" }`, the volatile tail as a second. `RunThreadOpts.prompt` and `ThreadOpts.seed` widen from `string` to `string | Anthropic.ContentBlockParam[]`; `Thread.messages` already drops the seed, so nothing renders it. The backend forwards `MessageCreateParams` unexamined, so nothing there changes.

**The prompt is a reflection, not an extraction.** `REFLECT_SYSTEM` reframes the job: you are looking at one interaction, in the context of a graph that already exists; what domain concepts does it touch, are they in the graph, what understanding did the user demonstrate, and does anything here read as a gap or a misconception. Then the restraint clauses, which are what actually control output size: touch only what this interaction is about; keep the graph small and coarse; split a concept only when the split expresses something real about this user's understanding; a concept the user merely brushed past does not need a node.

**Citations ground the notes.** A note that says "shaky on websocket framing" is unfalsifiable; a note that says it and points at the turn where the user said so is evidence. Every rendered transcript block carries its address — `@message:t0:3`, the thread id the tree already mints plus the index into `Thread.messages` — and `REFLECT_SYSTEM` requires that a claim about the user's understanding cite the interaction it came from. The address is free: the dispatch knows exactly which thread and index it is reflecting on.

The DSL is deliberately one token with no delimiters or link text. It survives round-tripping through a textarea, the model cannot get the syntax subtly wrong, and a stale or malformed reference degrades to literal text rather than to a broken render.

**Rendering: chips beside the field, not links inside it.** The sidebar edits `description` and `notes` in textareas, and a textarea cannot contain a link. Rather than build a rich-text editor for a prototype, each field gets a row of citation chips below it, one per reference in the *saved* text, labelled with the quote it points at (truncated). This stays inside vamp's `bindList`, keeps editing plain-text, and is arguably better than inline links: the chips are a bibliography for the claim.

**Navigation.** Clicking a chip switches to the threads tab, focuses the cited thread, and scrolls its transcript to the cited message with a brief flash. Focusing a deep thread means walking `tree.path(id)` and setting each ancestor's `activeChild`, which is what the two-pane layout reads — the same state `MARK_CLICKED` already manipulates, so no new notion of focus is introduced. A citation that does not resolve renders as inert text; nothing in the graph is validated against the tree.

**The build button goes away.** With reflection on every interaction there is nothing left for it to do, and a batch pass would double-count everything the live reflections already recorded. `Build`, `runBuild` and the toolbar status line are deleted. The graph tab becomes a pure view of a thing maintained elsewhere. `window.__graph` stays: the sidebar specs still need to seed a deterministic graph.

Alternatives rejected: reflecting on thread *close* or on some idle timer (there is no close, and an idle timer is a batch with extra steps); running the reflection as a tool call inside the learning thread (it would spend the user's latency and put the student model in the same context as the answer, which is exactly the entanglement the two-mode split exists to avoid); parallel reflections (duplicate nodes, as above).

- Every user interaction produces exactly one reflection: one per submitted turn, one per opened learning thread. Nothing is reflected on twice, and nothing reflects on the agent's own turns.

- A failed reflection does not corrupt the graph; the graph is only ever changed through `writeTools`.

- Citation indices are indices into `Thread.messages`, which is append-only, so an address stays valid for the life of the page. Nothing renumbers it.

Two candidate address spaces:

- **`Message` (current):** the projected transcript block. It's what the UI renders, and it's already the codebase's addressing convention — `selection.ts`'s `Point.msg` indexes exactly this, so citations and highlights would speak the same language. The weakness is that it's *derived*: `project()` drops `tool_result` blocks, hides the seed, and warns-and-drops content types it doesn't know (thinking blocks). Tool calls also have real ids there (`toolu_…`), so `@tool:<id>` would be a genuinely stable, self-describing address for the "the agent ran this command" case — no index arithmetic at all.
